en: *The Record of the Meaning of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Four.

If nature were subsumed within the three periods of time, it would be impermanent. From the fourth section, beginning with "If those who have severed their roots of goodness possess the Buddha-nature," and so forth, the question is posed based on the fixed notions of "definitely existing" and "definitely non-existing. This is for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the section "There are four kinds of answers" and below:
first, the reason for clarifying the four answers of former times is,
firstly, to clarify that by means of the past, the present is revealed.
The second is to clarify that the present is different from the past.
From "the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses" onwards,
up until the six brief mentions, it is called the "analytical answer."
This is intended to answer the first question.
First, the conditions are presented as they were previously stated: "As you asked before."
This answers the first question.

The intent of the answer is that those who have severed their roots of goodness (samucchinna-kuśalamūla) actually possess both types of Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) for their future bodies as Tathāgatas;
however, because they are currently obstructed by the causal conditions of false views, it is said that they do not possess them.
"The Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is not of the past," and so forth,
answers the third question by clarifying that the primary cause (正因) is eternal and does not belong to the three periods of time.
"The buddha-nature of the final body is present and future," and so forth.
I answer the second question;
herein, I constantly provide answers to the third question as well.
This is why it was placed at the beginning.
The answer to the third question is intended to clarify that the true cause does not belong to the three periods of time;
this is because it explains the meaning of the "increase by one" (*ekottara*) across nine stages, spanning the two periods of the final body and the three periods of the preceding lives.
Regarding the two lifetimes of the subsequent existence:
one takes the initial mind capable of seeing as the present, and from that point onward,
the succeeding minds of seeing are bound together to constitute the truth.
Regarding the fact that the Buddha-nature, as the cause [of Buddhahood], is subsumed within the three periods of time even before one has attained bodhi in the future:
this refers to the stage of outflows (sāsrava) prior to the first bhūmi.
Because these unwholesome five aggregates are the cause of the Buddha-nature, they are subsumed within the three periods of time; however, the fruit is not so.
There are those that belong to the three periods of time and those that do not:
this refers to the stages from the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi.
These wholesome five aggregates are the fruit of the unwholesome five aggregates; because their substance is impermanent, they are subsumed within the three periods of time.
The five aggregates of the Buddha-fruit are wholesome five aggregates.
Because the essence of the fruit is eternally abiding, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
From the ten stages down to the sixth dwelling, one clarifies the causes of the Buddha;
the same principle applies to the past, present, and future fruits as well.
From the fifth dwelling to the first dwelling...
[omitted] ...the fruits of the past, present, and future are likewise.
Because the meaning is the same as before... [omitted] ...the natures are of six kinds and seven kinds.

In this [passage], it is clarified that those who possess the highest degree of *icchantika* (those who have severed all roots of goodness) shall indeed exist. As for the fourth question, "I also do not say... [and so forth].
Furthermore, not answering by setting aside a question through partial explanation is called "setting aside" (*sthāpanīya*).
There is also the case where explaining away false conceptualizations (*parikalpita*) is called "setting aside.
What is meant by "reason" (*hetu*)?
Regarding the past, present, and future:
since these are intended to be assigned to persons,
he therefore asks this question.
Furthermore, it was stated above that the causes and effects of the three periods of time and the non-three periods of time were explained in detail.
Now, the intent of the question is to inquire why the cause exists across the three periods of time, and why the effect exists both within the three periods of time and outside of them.

The answer is that because the causes—the unwholesome five aggregates—are comprised within the three periods of time, their results—both the unwholesome five aggregates and the wholesome five aggregates—likewise exist within the three periods of time; thus, there are the three periods of time.
From this point downward, there is a detailed explanation of the distinction between the three periods of time and that which is not comprised within the three periods of time.
From the section beginning with "All ignorance" (*avidyā*) and below, there are three parts in total.
These extensively explain how the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*) is subsumed under the three periods of time, whereas the substantial cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) is not so subsumed.

The first section directly addresses the principle to extensively clarify that the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) are subsumed within the three time periods, whereas the primary cause (*hetu-hetu*) is not subsumed by the time periods. Below this...
The second [section] cites the sutras to clarify whether the conditions and the correct [path] encompass or do not encompass [the result],
starting from the stage of the *srotāpanna* downward.
The third [section] clarifies whether the conditions and the correct [path] encompass or do not encompass [the result] by way of the person.
Regarding the statement that "śrāvakas are like milk":
because the Tathāgata above intends to establish the meaning of the *Ekottarika-āgama*,
he explains it by proceeding downward from the Buddha.
In this context, in order to establish that what precedes is subtle and what follows is manifest,
they are explained by proceeding from the bottom upward.
The lower grade of the Ten Abodes constitutes the Pratyekabuddha.
Those of the highest grade are bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, what meaning does the phrase "those who will exist in the future in five, six, or seven births" clarify?
The preceding section has merely clarified that the two types of Buddha-nature—conditional and immediate—give rise to wholesome qualities.
From here on, the meaning of how they give rise to wholesome qualities is explained.
Regarding future karma, whether it has already arisen or not yet arisen, it ultimately does not produce a fruit.
It is to clarify that the Buddha-nature of the future necessarily exists;
therefore, it can produce present goodness, which is unlike future karma.
Furthermore, it is said that this future karma does not exist [yet].
It cannot produce its fruit.
There currently exists an inferior-grade cause that will necessarily produce a medium-grade karma in the future,
because at some point in the future it will necessarily attain the production of its fruit.
It is called "having Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, because it does not yet exist, it is not said to exist presently;
because it will certainly exist, it is called "will exist."
Because that which is to be (bhavāgra) exists, it brings about the excellence of the present life;
however, due to superior karma in the future,
because that has not yet arisen, it will ultimately not produce a fruit.
One might raise the objection that since the Buddha-nature of future Buddhas does not yet exist at this very moment,
how can it give rise to wholesome qualities? Below,
two analogies are used to illustrate the principle of its arising.
If it is said that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature,
from here below the text returns to its primary thesis to extensively clarify the Middle Way principle of neither existence nor non-existence as the Buddha-nature.
This is the second response to the fourth question above,
clarifying that [the nature of things] is neither definitively existent nor definitively non-existent.
From here below, the text will clarify the generation of wholesome states.
Some prior adherents may maintain that this is for the purpose of clarifying the Middle Way,
as it is the root from which wholesome qualities arise;
they hold that the existing aggregates constitute its intrinsic nature.
The question merely addresses the grasping at a single instance;
in reality, it extensively raises many doubts.
Because one clings to conditions as being ultimate reality, it is said that sentient beings who have lost the Way do not understand.
This refers to the Middle Way, which clarifies that because there is no understanding, Buddha-nature does not manifest.

This is not a case of it being non-existent; rather, at times there is understanding, clarifying that Buddha-nature is not entirely absent. Thus, being neither existent nor non-existent constitutes the Middle Way.
I act for the sake of sentient beings who have attained understanding;
yet those who cling to the existence or non-existence of the internal and external lack such understanding.
Below, it is clarified that what is neither internal nor external is like empty space or a rabbit’s horn.
By means of six similes, he clarifies that [reality] is neither existent nor non-existent, causing understanding to arise; this is for the purpose of opening up comprehension.
Regarding the one with a fever who drinks milk:
The commentary states:
In foreign lands, milk is cold while curd is hot; therefore, consuming milk removes heat-related illnesses.
However, consuming it in excess gives rise to cold-related illnesses.
Consuming milk curd can eliminate cold-natured illnesses;
however, if consumed in excess, it conversely produces heat-natured illnesses.
According to this principle, if the milk is hot-natured, the curd will be cold-natured.
As for those who say that one suffering from a feverish illness should consume milk, this means treating heat with heat.
For those with a downward-flowing illness (diarrhea) who consume curd, this is treating cold with cold. Milk produces cold illnesses.
This clarifies that milk is not only able to cure feverish diseases when it arises, but can also cure cold-natured diseases;
the subsequent statement that curd produces feverish diseases follows the same principle.
If it is argued that the five tastes first arise depending on conditions,
just as the internal great elements (mahābhūtas) first depend on the external great elements,
this is logically untenable. Why is this so?
Because the five flavors are explained according to their sequential order,
curd and clarified butter are not produced from various conditions; rather, they arise from milk through two specific conditions.
Up to and including *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter), all dharmas are not like this;
they are obtained solely from two conditions.
That which is not attained through skillful means is not correct;
it can be attained through two types of skillful means,
and specifically through five conditions.
That which can increase the four great elements internally and externally is likewise thus:
all are originally non-existent and arise from conditions.
Furthermore, it says that by means of grasping and calculation, one refutes the externalist's reckoning of the cause within the milk.
Just as curdled milk already exists and does not depend on expedient means to first produce it,
so too is the Buddha-nature.
To claim that it pre-exists within the body and is not obtained through conditions is merely a false conceptualization.
As for my [view that] *sattva*, *adharma*, *jīva*, and so forth are not like this:
they do not exist beforehand; it is made clear through skillful means (*upāya*) that their essence is originally non-existent and is only attained through skillful means.
The four great elements and the Buddha-nature are all likewise dependent upon conditions for their service.
From what I have taught in the twelve divisions of the sutras down to those who exclusively pursue intellectual understanding—
this clarifies that biased attachment constitutes a sickness.
This is to encourage faith in the Middle Way so that goodness may arise.
Furthermore, it is to clarify that even the teachings on impermanence found in past sutras— which were spoken according to the Buddha’s own intentions—
can still lead one to produce understanding.
How much more so now, when explaining the Buddha-nature through discourse that accords with one's own mind—how could understanding not arise?
Even regarding whether the Buddha-nature exists or does not exist in the icchantika, it is the same:

this clarifies that at the time the icchantika attains Buddhahood, the existence or non-existence of their Buddha-nature is identical to the existence or non-existence of the present Buddha, differing in no way whatsoever.
It is also said that for an icchantika, present evil exists, while the absence of good is what is meant by "non-existence.
Formerly, when discussing the emptiness of nature with Maitreya, it was regarded as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
however, because the principle of emptiness is profound and mysterious, it is [here] considered ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Śāriputra and others were unable to give rise to understanding;
however, the reason Subhūti and others were able to speak for the sake of the great bodhisattvas was due to the inspiration of the Tathāgata.
Even regarding the conventional truth within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they still did not understand.
How much more so regarding the Buddha-nature, which is supreme,
yet you have instead followed your own inclinations to reach a one-sided understanding, rather than following the Buddha's words.
Furthermore, it says:
Śāriputra is indeed a person of great expedient power (mahopāya).
It is not that he lacks understanding; rather, he assumes the appearance of a true śrāvaka in accordance with the traces he manifests.
This is as described in the passage beginning with "In the Ganges River there are seven classes of sentient beings," and so forth.
This third major section of the chapter clarifies the meaning of abandoning [defilements] by means of analogies drawn from above.
If one is unable to understand the meaning within these four preceding propositions,
one will become like the two types of persons mentioned before.
If one can understand this, one should perform it in successive succession.
Regarding the "five subtle rivers" mentioned later:
in the section on the superior grade, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are treated as the river.
Birth and death constitute the water.
Within this, the teaching of nirvāṇa serves as the river,
and the four kinds of buddha-nature serve as the water.
The former exhorted the cultivation of the Way and the realization of one's nature to attain immediate results;
the present passage exhorts the understanding of Buddha-nature to achieve the status of the latter five types of people.
The former clarifies that those unable to cultivate the Way sink into the cycle of birth and death.
This is also to be lost within the dharma of nirvana;
herein, to be lost within the principle and teaching of nirvana is likewise to be lost within the river of birth and death.
For now, one side of each has been cited to mutually clarify their meaning.
The same applies to the seven types of persons.
Herein, two sets of seven types of persons are enumerated;
those of the superior grade are not listed.
This is also merely a mutual clarification.
As for the three types of people mentioned above, they are those who do not cultivate the three kinds of goodness and so forth.
Furthermore, there are those who are constantly submerged who are not *icchantikas*.
These are the three types of people who delight in the three realms of existence and are submerged therein.
Among those who are generally submerged, there are some who are icchantikas and others who are like the person wearing the jewel who is submerged.
There are those who exist within the three realms of existence yet are not icchantikas;
likewise, there are those who emerge for a moment only to sink back down.
Furthermore, there are those who are perpetually submerged, yet are not icchantikas.
Regarding the reference to Shanxing and others below:

if this person can recite the twelve [dharmas] and practice various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), they are called one who "delights in the three realms of existence" and is the second type of person;
if they sever their roots of goodness, they are the first type of person.
It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because from contaminated precepts one gives rise to uncontaminated precepts.
Precept refers to that which a person has not yet fully realized as complete.
That which is capable of drawing forth a resultant name is termed "active precept" (*kriyā-śīla*).
Not perceiving birth and death constitutes the unconditioned precept (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*).
The precept that follows the Path and turns its back on birth and death is called the "precept of relinquishment" (*tyāga-śīla*).
This is why the stage of the "nature of practice" (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*) is not listed as one of the abiding stages of persons.
They are not listed because, within that category, there are those who regress and those who do not, due to its broad and diffuse nature.
As for the reason why the third type of person is listed at the end of the section on abiding,
and the subsequent five types are not listed, it is because from this point onward, it can be understood that there are no longer any who are not persons abiding.
There are five matters by which wisdom is not fully perfected;
these have already been clarified previously in the case of Śāriputra and others.
The present section concerns those who abide [in the path].
Below this, the abiding persons are explained in detail;
because they practiced in former times, they have subsequently attained accomplishment.

One subdues greed through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and each of the afflictions is subdued by its respective antidote, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).

As for the discursive thoughts that cause distress, many practitioners employ the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) to universally subdue the ten underlying tendencies (*daśānuśaya*); those who are strongly attached to a self [should likewise apply this].
Analyzing the elements and sense bases:

all these people seek within the factors of dhyāna to cultivate such contemplations; their minds manifest detachment from evil, they seek the foundation of dhyāna nearby, and they aspire to be born in the realm of emptiness afar.
"Those who have heard this" refers to all the aforementioned individuals who, having heard this skillful reversal that explains the method of contemplation,
have already attained the fundamental practice of the contemplation on the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Initially, one correctly contemplates the five aggregates as suffering due to disintegration and as impermanent due to disintegration;
furthermore, knowing that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one continues this contemplation until it is perfected.
One then correctly contemplates the emptiness of persons while simultaneously understanding that sentient beings are composed of the five aggregates.
"Practicing according to the Dharma" refers to the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
"Subsequently attaining the applications of mindfulness" refers to entering individually into the four emptinesses (*catasraḥ śūnyatāḥ*).

First, one correctly contemplates the physical body as suffering through transformation, as subject to decay, and as impermanent, while simultaneously knowing that the body lacks intrinsic nature; as this contemplation continues, one correctly contemplates the emptiness of the body while simultaneously knowing the body [as such].

This is called the application of the contemplation of the body as suffering through transformation, impermanence, and emptiness. Once this is established, the same applies to the [remaining] three [contemplations].
This is the beginning of wisdom through reflection.
For those of dull faculties, one next applies right effort and subsequently practices the contemplation of "as one wishes.
Only then can one integrate the four foundations of mindfulness into the single sphere of a single dharma.

By practicing the asceticism of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) while simultaneously understanding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one enters the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
This is the beginning of the inclination toward emptiness during the stages of hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*),

wherein one must first cultivate the contemplation of the destruction of suffering and the destruction of impermanence, while concurrently realizing the absence of intrinsic nature, in order to move toward the direct perception of this contemplation of emptiness.

From the beginning up to the Arhat, one must practice the essential asceticism of conditioned suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) while simultaneously understanding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in order to enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As for the sequence of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in the text:
This must refer to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it is those of the Middle Vehicle with sharp faculties who perform this contemplation.
However, those of the Middle Vehicle contemplate directly the nature of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, by means of the lack of intrinsic nature in dependent origination, one enters into emptiness; this differs from the contemplation of suffering in the Lesser Vehicle mentioned previously.
Within this [system], there are these three faculties.
Now, in this context, the twelve links of dependent origination are presented following the foundations of mindfulness.
This refers to those of sharp, medium, and inferior faculties.
However, since the application of mindfulness to the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-smṛtyupasthāna) is practiced by both the sharp and the dull,
those of sharp, medium, and inferior faculties likewise perform this contemplation.
However, they do not personally practice the contemplation of the suffering of change.
If those of middling or superior capacity do not practice the contemplation of the application of mindfulness on the emptiness of persons,
they directly practice the contemplation of the causes and conditions of the three periods of time.
By entering the emptiness of phenomena and emerging from the emptiness of phenomena,
one already knows that sentient beings are also empty;
this is still the level of inferior faculties.
Entering first by way of the emptiness of sentient beings and emerging with the knowledge that all phenomena are void:
entering is without difficulty;
this is for those of sharp, middling, and inferior faculties who emerge from the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Subsequently, one contemplates the twelve links in reverse order, observing the specific conditions of dependent origination;
this is done while simultaneously practicing the contemplation of disintegration and impermanence, as well as the absence of intrinsic nature within dependent origination.
Alternatively, while correctly deconstructing the absence of a locus, one simultaneously acts as the causal condition;
and by means of the lack of intrinsic nature in causes and conditions, one enters the emptiness of causes and conditions.
This is still merely an intellectual understanding that has not yet become manifest.
From this contemplation, one further contemplates the three periods of time in general as constituting past causes and conditions,
present causes and conditions,
and simultaneously practicing the impermanence of formations.
It also simultaneously possesses the naturelessness of causes and conditions;
or, while performing the activity of impermanence, it simultaneously acts as a cause and condition,
and thus also simultaneously possesses the naturelessness of causes and conditions.
Entering into the emptiness of causes and conditions, one achieves the realization of "Heat" and "Summit" through direct perception.
One who practices the contemplation of the forty-four knowledges possesses sharp faculties of middling capacity;
one who practices the contemplation of the seventy-seven knowledges possesses sharp faculties of superior capacity.

As for these two individuals, their application of the contemplative method regarding the causal conditions of the three periods of time and the departure from conceptualization is as previously described;
yet there is a further distinction:
namely, that within the understanding of this aforementioned contemplation of departure, there are two grades, the initial and the final.
The inferior grade constitutes the wisdom of hearing;
the superior grade constitutes the wisdom of reflection;
and the comprehensive contemplation from the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) up to the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) constitutes the wisdom of cultivation.
Those of inferior faculties give rise to the understanding of the emptiness of persons;
this is their wisdom derived from hearing.
It is for this reason that they differ.
Among the sixteen aspects, non-Buddhists possess only six aspects— namely,
the four aspects of origination (*samudaya*) and the two aspects of suffering (*duḥkha*)— and therefore they lack the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage.
Furthermore, it is said that they observe only these six aspects.
One feels weary of the three lower modes of practice—impermanence, suffering, and impurity—and takes delight in the three higher modes of practice—permanence, bliss, and purity.
For this reason, there is no "heat" (ūṣmagata).
My disciples who are fully endowed with these sixteen [aspects] [attain it].
Because those outsiders employ those respective knowledges within the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience,
they perform the sixteen aspects of contemplation from beginning to end.
However, according to the correct meaning, regarding the four minds of Heat and so forth:
Because there is also such practice, it is not incorrect.
Regarding those who obtain the five aggregates of the form realm as a retribution for the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) mind:
if one interprets this as being reborn in the higher realms, [it would be so].

Because the preceding "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) mind suppresses the fetters of desire, the mind that emerges from contemplation subsequently gives rise to craving for the first dhyāna, thereby receiving the retribution of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If one were to interpret this as not being reborn in higher realms, [it would contradict the sūtras].
With "heat" (*uṣmagata*) as its cause,
one relies upon the four dhyānas to give rise to that superior heat;
however, this contemplation is precisely the fifth aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) of that stage.
If the four formless attainments (ārūpya) were to give rise to "heat" (uṣmagata), the meaning would be the same.
For now, we shall discuss only the five aggregates (skandha) of the form realm obtained as karmic retribution.
As for "heat," it is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma).

If one adopts the former interpretation, it means that following the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), the arising of craving for the first dhyāna constitutes birth in the realm of form (rūpadhātu); thus, it is called "existence" (bhava) because it is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛtadharma).
Subsequently, when "Heat" gives rise to the fetters (saṃyojana), it is called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) because it is produced by outflows (āsrava).
Furthermore, it can destroy conditioned and out-flowing (sāsrava) phenomena.

Although one emerges from meditative absorption and gives rise to craving, experiencing the retribution of form-ground (rūpa-bhūmi), because of the preceding contemplation that understands [phenomena] as being produced by causes,
and due to the subsequent superior contemplation, one is able to destroy them.

If one adopts the latter interpretation, it is said that "there is a dharma" because the *uṣmagata* (heat) of that form realm (*rūpadhātu*) arises with the *uṣmagata* of the present life as its cause;
"conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is as explained previously.
If this is so, then [the subsequent heat] arises from the previous out-flowing (*āsrava*) *uṣmagata*.
Subsequently, the outflow-tainted heat (*uṣmagata*) continues in an uninterrupted succession;
it is able to give rise to the outflow-free [states] that destroy the outflow-tainted, conditioned practices—the answer to the following question may be understood from this.
"Both affectionate and exhortative" means:
Because one maintains the aggregates (*skandha*) upon emerging from contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and because entering contemplation to discern emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called "exertion" (*pragraha*).
Regarding those who have attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) through the Dharma, there are seventy-three types.
The preceding section clarified the factors of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*); this section now clarifies the person who practices the factors of "peak" (*mūrdhan*).
Regarding the afflictions of the desire realm, they are divided into nine grades.
If one has subdued one grade, they constitute one person; if all nine grades have been subdued, they constitute nine persons.
If none have yet been subdued, they again constitute one person, making ten persons in total.
From the initial stage of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the middle portion of these stages is divided into nine levels.
Based on their respective degrees of subduing [the afflictions], there are nine types of persons for each.
Thus, seven times nine makes sixty-three; when added to the ten [paths] directed toward the desire realm, they total seventy-three persons.

The reason the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is not discussed is that outsiders falsely claim that once one has severed the lower stages above [the form realm], there is no further meditative ground (dhyāna-bhūmi) beyond the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Because non-Buddhists cannot subdue the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are not discussed here.

It is clarified that such individuals, while still at the stage of external ordinary persons (bāhyapṛthagjana), cultivate dhyāna to subdue their fetters, and subsequently enter the stage of internal ordinary persons (adhyātmikapṛthagjana) to practice the sixteen aspects of contemplation and enter the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
These two types of persons refer to those who are directed toward the five matters.
Even if one person does not possess all five, provided they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*),
they will gradually enter the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and, as a resident of that stage, ultimately attain the fruit of the noble ones (*āryaphala*).

If a single person lacks five things, and furthermore encounters evil friends who incite them toward grave evils, they will sink into the four realms of existence; this is what is meant by "submerging once more.
The general meaning is extensively illustrated through further citations.
Regarding those five people of the past:
first, one of them serves as the foundation for the present teaching;
second, this demonstrates from afar that all five people of the past possess Buddha-nature.
It was simply that it could not be spoken of in the past.
Although the stage of the summit (mūrdha-dharma) is by nature the five aggregates, it is nevertheless capable of performing the analytical contemplation of the four noble truths.
It is said that [the nature of] speech also takes the four truths as its object.
Regarding these five faculties (*indriya*), the word "this" (*shi*) is an error;
according to principle, it should also be stated that their nature consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The reason for this is that,
through this first dharma, one can successively attain the retribution of the form realm (rūpadhātu);
yet, its very substance is still the outflowing five aggregates (sāsrava-pañcaskandha).
Therefore, one should not say that the nature [of the self] is the five aggregates and the sense faculties.
Furthermore, regarding those who rely on the Four Noble Truths:
formerly, while still at the stage of an ordinary person, they had not yet witnessed the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates.

To hold that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) exists determinately and is eternal is to claim it does not arise from causes; this is delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering and also delusion regarding the Truth of Origination.
If its nature were existent and eternal, it could not be extinguished.
This constitutes delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation;
since the Path is useless with respect to the nature [of things], it constitutes delusion regarding the Truth of the Path.
Thus, one is deluded regarding all four truths simultaneously.

Now, if one practices and attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) or above, one perceives that the body of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus one penetrates [this truth].
Because one understands that suffering arises from causes and that the Path can extinguish these burdens, it is said that one also takes the four truths as conditions.

Regarding why it is called "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the explanation states that, generally speaking, there are three ways in the world to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The first is to sever them through the suppression of aversion rather than through the removal [of defilements] via principle; this refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The second consists of those who follow both from weariness and from principle; these are the followers of the Two Vehicles.
The third consists of those who follow from principle but not from weariness;
these are the Bodhisattvas.
Because Bodhisattvas follow only the principle,
they are given the name "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" based on that principle;
whereas Śrāvakas enter emptiness by way of revulsion toward suffering.
Therefore, by penetrating suffering, it is designated as the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
This patience regarding the dharma of suffering exists within the practice of signlessness (*animitta-caryā*);
because one perceives the equality of the four noble truths, it is called the nature of patience.
This wisdom takes the Single Truth as its object.
These three stages are called "repeated" because they serve as the foundation for others.
The text also states that they encompass all fetters to be abandoned.
A brief explanation of the underlying meanings:

the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) serves as the basis for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) serves as the basis for attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and doubt (*vicikitsā*) serves as the basis for false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
These three superior factors are the root [defilements] within the [list of] fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are established later.

These three arise throughout both the preceding and succeeding stages as that which is constantly produced; although the mind of great false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) does not give rise to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), [it functions in this manner].
However, those with minor wrong views lack any aspiration for supramundane *nirvāṇa*;
they still cling to the existence of a *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* (the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) as *nirvāṇa*,
and thus arrogantly conceive themselves as undergoing rebirth.
This constitutes the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
Because it permeates the other four views, it is termed "that which is constantly arisen.
It can give rise to the other [views], or because its underlying principle is obscure, it is subtle and difficult to discern.
It is further said:

Those that arise constantly—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—are called "subtle and difficult to recognize" because they are not coarse and thus not easily removed; being fundamentally fine, they are difficult to dispel, and therefore difficult to sever.
These three remedies are merely designated as "intermediate" for the time being;
in reality, the ten afflictions (daśa-āsrava) pervade all three Piṭakas.
Regarding the two kinds of names:
When one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is the name "flowing with the current," which is called the "original name.

Later, upon becoming a *srotāpanna*, one first attains the name "flowing against the current," which is considered a "guest name. As for the phrase "because it was obtained first": [it refers to the former state].
Srotāpanna regains its original name because it is attained later; as for Sakṛdāgāmin,
its name is established later, and therefore it is called "guest."
There are two kinds of outflows:
first, liberation, which is the untainted (anāsrava) contemplative understanding;
second, nirvāṇa, which is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) cessation of fetters.
Therefore, the commentator explains that all sages possess these two attainments, and for this reason they are established under the same name.
This applies from those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna (Stream-enterer) down to those called Bodhisattvas.
The preceding section clarified that the names of the higher [realms] can be applied to the lower;
from this point onward, it further clarifies that the names of the lower [realms] can likewise be applied to the higher.
While the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are shared, their realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not shared.
It is also said that while the [truths of] suffering and its origin are shared with ordinary beings, the path is called "unshared.
Regarding the sixteen aspects:
there are four under the heading of suffering.
These are the so-called [contemplations of] suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self;
continuing thus down to the four aspects of the Path,
these four sets of four together constitute sixteen.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that there are sixteen [moments] directed toward the fruit: taken collectively, there are sixteen;
however, if one distinguishes them according to the meaning of the individuals who enter the Path through the suffering [of the desire realm], [there are more].
It is not for the sake of impermanence and so forth.
Why is it that those who enter the Path through impermanence do not delight in the human condition as suffering, yet instead observe it accordingly?
Since the case for suffering at the lower level is thus established, the same applies by analogy to the other three truths. Taken collectively, there are sixteen aspects;
however, when analyzed individually, within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), there are only four contemplations of the Truths and not twelve modes of activity.
Regarding the statement that there are sixteen aspects of the untainted (anāsrava),
these do not constitute sixteen within the practice of signlessness (animitta);
rather, they are called the sixteen aspects because one contemplates the emptiness of the sixteen objects as a whole.
This can be understood from among the sixteen types of practice within the fruit.

"Having fully observed and practiced" refers to the *sakṛdāgāmin* who, having advanced in superior insight (*vipaśyanā*), abandons the three subtle grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to attain the higher fruit; this is called "having fully observed and practiced."
There are two kinds:
first, that which exhausts the fetters by consuming the three fruits;
second, that which is cultivated through nutriment.
The untainted [path] causes the life-force of wisdom to continue uninterrupted.
Because one has severed the three subtle fetters and attained the fruit of Anāgāmin, dwelling in the higher realms, it is called "abiding.
There are two kinds of this.
In summary, the Anāgāmins are categorized into two types:
those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life constitute one type,
while all others who are reborn in higher realms constitute the other type.
Although the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not itself the realm of form,
because it is directed toward the realm of form, it is entirely included within the realm of form.
The first type consists of those who, having attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin) in the present life, further cultivate practice to attain arhatship.
This sentence is a general statement.

Within it, there are those who enter meditative contemplation from the mind of the fruit of anāgāmin and thereby become an asaṅga (one free from attachment), as well as those who enter and emerge from the contemplation of emptiness and thereby become an arhat.
The subsequent statement regarding the addition of "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" refers to those who enter meditative contemplation from the fruit-mind and thereby achieve it;
it is also intended to demonstrate the differences among the five types of persons regarding their attainment of parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Furthermore, regarding those who attain nirvana without an element (anupādisesa-nibbāna):
having been born among the Bṛhatphala deities,
after their lives there end, they transcend the five realms of form and are reborn in the formless realm.
Furthermore, *parinirvāṇa* refers specifically to those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One should also say that among the five heavens, there are those who attain *parinirvāṇa*.
However, because those who delight in wisdom share the same realm (*dhātu*), they are omitted and not explicitly mentioned.
The following text will naturally explain how these two types of persons attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there are two kinds," this is cited as an illustration to clarify the upward-streamer (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
This does not mean that the preceding section on *antarāparinirvāyin* has already been explained; the subsequent passage concerning *upapadyaparinirvāyin* will be explained separately.
The reason for citing the *ūrdhvasrotas* here is as follows:
The above discussion concerned those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state without further rebirth;
now, to clarify those in the formless realm,
they are indeed situated in the stage of "upward-streaming" (ūrdhvasrotas).
One who does not become an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) takes only two or four bodies within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
In the treatise (*śāstra*), such a person as an Upstreamer is not established as a separate category;
however, here, by means of the fivefold method of exposition, they are so established.
Among the four types of bodies, those who receive two [of the three trainings] are of sharp faculties;
those who receive three are of middling faculties;
and those who receive four are of dull faculties.
Receiving one [birth] refers to the three types of persons within the realm of rebirth (*upapadya*).
Therefore, it is said that receiving two up to four births constitutes the "one who flows upward" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Because they exercise mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and give rise to contemplation of the principle (*tattva*), it is called "mastery of concentration" (*vaśitā-samādhi*).

Regarding the "one who performs karma," this refers to the time when one is still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) prior to becoming a non-returner (anāgāmin); it is at that time that one creates this karma with ignorance and grasping as conditions.
Regarding the "one who does not undergo rebirth," there is no defiled attachment.
In the birthplaces of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), one gives rise to deluded craving that moistens karma and brings about retribution.
This is because those seeking birth therein do not delight in being born in the higher realms during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

However, this karmic retribution of the intermediate state is created during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); such a person possesses both the karma for birth and the subsequent karma, and thus experiences both.
Because the two minds pertain to the beginning and end of the Arhat’s state, they collectively comprise four minds.
For now, I have clarified these four minds with reference to the beginning of the intermediate parinirvāṇa and the higher rebirth;
however, all other types of Anāgāmins may likewise be explained.

Now, since this section clarifies only those who attain rebirth in higher realms after the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it does not clarify those who undergo transmigration; thus, they may be omitted.

Furthermore, as for the three types of persons who have realized through the body (*kāyāsākṣin*) and attained conviction, their significance applies generally to others as well, and therefore they are not discussed here.
The section beginning with "Having attained nirvana in this body" explains the three types of persons among those born above; thus,
it clarifies the sharp and dull faculties of these three types within a single lifetime, which accords with the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*.
Regarding the statement "producing karma within the body of experience":
this refers to the karma that produces the retribution of birth in the First Dhyāna.
Because of this karma, one has not yet attained the fruit of sainthood.

Regarding the statement that "in general, no karma for rebirth is created during the preceding intermediate state (*antarābhava*)," this clarifies that such karma is not created within the body of a *naivāsika* (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state).
As for the statement that "no karma for rebirth is created now," it means [that such karma is not created] in the present life.
The karma created during ordinary times that results in rebirth in the next life,
and the karma for rebirth in the first dhyāna— each of these is categorized according to its specific aspect; yet,
in reality, it is through these that one takes birth.
One is then able to become weary of suffering, enter meditative contemplation, sever the outflows, and attain the state of an Arhat, realizing *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
What is now called "entering nirvāṇa at the end of one's lifespan" refers to entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The treatise states that those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) are spoken of in terms of realizing *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This [present discussion], however, refers to *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; because the former and latter differ, the question arises.

The meaning of the subsequent answer is that once one has received a body and severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, one becomes an arhat and realizes *sopadhiśeṇa-nirvāṇa*, which does not contradict the treatises or the sūtras.
Regarding "attaining nirvāṇa within the course of practice," this clarifies that one who is able to sever the afflictions and enter nirvāṇa realizes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
"Without practice" (asaṃskāra) actually benefits those who attain parinirvāṇa through practice; its realization is identical to that discussed in the *Sūtra on the Attainment of Nirvāṇa*.
The statement that "now, with the end of his lifespan, he enters nirvana" refers to entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
As for "the one who attains nirvana by ascending," the following sections provide a sequential explanation according to the headings of this chapter.

Furthermore, distinguishing between the differences in aversion and pleasure: when one regresses from birth, it may sometimes not transcend the craving for the first dhyāna until one has first arisen in the fourth dhyāna and subsequently in the third dhyāna.
Only after being born into the second dhyāna does one first give rise to craving for the first dhyāna;
the present statement regarding "craving for the first dhyāna" is spoken from the perspective of reaching the same level.
The *Abhidharma* says "not cumbersome" (*avṛha*), whereas this [text] says "Slightless" (*atapa*). That [term] explains from below upward;
here, it explains from above downward.
Therefore, he again clarifies the cultivation of *vāsanā-bhāvanā-dhyāna*.
Previously, it was stated that there are five stages in the cultivation of the fourth dhyāna;
now, the method of its cultivation is clarified.
This refers to the cultivation of perfuming (*vāsanā*), which differs from the Abhidharma system where perfuming is treated as a distinct entity.
However, for those who delight in wisdom, their aspiration is to cultivate meditation and develop insight, taking the exposition of principles as the foundation.
Those who cultivate the bliss of *vāsanā-dhyāna* (perfuming meditation) do not wish to generate wisdom or engage in doctrinal debate;
because they simply undergo rebirth according to their karma, they do not cultivate the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
These two types of persons belong to the stage of "upward-streaming" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) among others.
Since the two types of persons were distinguished within the section on the "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas),
this lower section clarifies those two persons;
having completed that, it returns to conclude the discussion on the Upstreamer.
Because those who delight in wisdom do not take birth there,
they censure the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
This applies to those who wish to enter the blissful concentration of the formless realm.
They should also be censured.
[The afflictions] within the five pure abodes are omitted and not explained here.
Regarding the two types of causes and conditions for the afflictions of the desire realm:
The first consists of the three afflictions of the internal mind;
the second consists of the seven evils of the external body and speech.
Because the higher realms possess only the three afflictions of the mind and lack the seven transgressions of body and speech, it is said that they have no "external" [afflictions].
Furthermore, in the higher realms, fetters arise within one's own internal body;
this is because afflictions arising from the bodies of others outside are few.
This applies to those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire.
Because his allotted lifespan was equal to that of ordinary people, it is said that he had not yet departed from them;
this refers to one of sharp faculties who has merely begun to depart from the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya).
Regarding lifespan, that which occupies the middle is the faculty of medium capacity (*madhya-indriya*).
As for those who reach the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), their lifespans are long and distant;
because this is similar to the retribution of form, it is said they "reach the limit."
This refers to those of dull faculties.
Regarding "having obtained food and remaining," there are six types of explanations below that clarify the meaning of obtaining food and remaining.
First, it clarifies that abiding within the three realms is called "dwelling";
furthermore, because one sustains the continuity of the two realms and receives life through nutriment, it is called "nutriment.
Second, it clarifies not receiving a body within the five destinies of the desire realm.
It may be said that he has exhausted the bodies of the five realms of existence and will not undergo them again; therefore, it is called "abiding.
He has already severed immeasurable afflictions.
Third, it clarifies that through the cessation of nutriment, the fetters of the seven dhyāna stages are exhausted;
because only the non-percipient state remains uneliminated, and one abides in the non-arising of the subtle and the intermediate, it is called "abiding.

Fourth, it clarifies that by withdrawing from nutriment, one exhausts the wholesome and unwholesome karmas that bind one to rebirth with ordinary beings; because one abides in the state of non-activity, it is said to be "abiding."
Fifth, because one is able to abide within the state where the causes and effects of birth and death for both self and others are not produced, it is called "abiding.
Sixth, because one’s food is free from the two cravings and greed and hatred are forever exhausted, abiding in this state of eternal detachment, it is called "abiding."
"Not departing from the water of Buddha-nature" summarizes that the two types of seven persons do not depart from the water of the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*).
"These seven sentient beings" and below summarize that the two types of seven persons do not depart from the water of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
If there is a cause, then there is a fruit.
The reason for this inquiry is that the aforementioned five unwholesome aggregates serve as the cause for the five wholesome aggregates.
This question arises because the five aggregates serve as the cause for the fruit of Buddhahood.
The intent of the question is that whatever has a cause must be impermanent; since nirvāṇa is permanent, it must be without cause.
Because it lacks a cause, it likewise lacks a fruit.
If there were no fruit of nirvāṇa, there would likewise be no primary cause (hetu).
If its nature were such, how could one attain the aforementioned statement that it is not separated from the water of the primary cause?
The answer below is as follows: although it does not arise from an originating cause (janakahetu), it is perceived through a revealing cause (jñāpakahetu) as the fruit of permanence.
Since the fruit is eternally abiding and possesses the water of the primary cause, it is not separate from it.
As for the fruit of skillful means (*upāya-phala*):
it is called the fruit of skillful means because it is attained through the application of human effort and activity in the present.

The fruit is named "karmic fruition" because it arises from past wholesome karma; it is also called the "fruition of present human effort," meaning the karmic activity performed through current exertion.
The subsequent statement that this is the "fruit of skillful means" is merely a brief explanation.
One should also say that this is called the fruit of karmic action.
That a child is able to provide care and support is called the fruit of gratitude.
Because it arises from the past virtuous karma of the parents, it is termed "proximate."
Based on the person of the filial son, the acts of bestowing kindness and providing nourishment are considered remote.
As for the remaining fruits:
first, the precept of non-killing, from its beginning to its end, is divided into two categories.
These constitute the two types of retribution:
the primary cause and the primary retribution,
which result in the fruits obtained in this present life.
The third type of bodily experience refers to the total and specific results of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives; these are collectively termed "residual fruits" (*avaśeṣa-phala*).

Generally speaking, regarding virtuous karma, the residual collective retribution cannot be experienced within the three miserable realms (*durgati*), though the residual specific retribution can be experienced there. The same applies to the residual retribution of non-virtuous karma.
Among human beings, one cannot receive the collective [result] but can only receive the individual [results].
What is now stated— such as "due to not killing"—
is a partial discussion of the remaining fruits of wholesome karma.

The proximate cause is the purification of the three karmas and the ten wholesome paths of action from the past; the remote cause consists of external substances that sustain the body, such as elixirs of immortality, which serve to prolong one's lifespan.
As for the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*):
This present medium-grade wholesome karma is the fruit and retribution of past low-grade causes;
this is the medium-grade wholesome [karma].
That which can produce superior-grade goodness refers precisely to this superior-grade goodness as the fruit within the category of retribution (*vipākaphala*). Here,
because this medium-grade goodness describes a past cause, it is termed "fruit."
However, because one desires that the fruits of past causes be inexhaustible in their future retribution,
and because these present intermediate-grade virtues can further produce superior-grade fruits—
thereby fulfilling the principle of the inexhaustibility of retribution for past virtuous causes— it is called "retribution" (*pāpa*).
Regarding "the proximate cause being the purity of body and speech in the present":
among the three types of karma in the present, wholesome karma of medium grade is called a "proximate cause" because it is proximate in relation to superior-grade karma of the present.
The wholesome karma of the three types of action from the past,
when compared to the superior [karma] of the present, is distant and serves as a remote cause.
As for the three gates of liberation acting as the non-arising cause for all afflictions:
To be able to sever the afflictions so that they never arise again is called "non-arising.
As for the term "arising" mentioned below, it refers to the capacity to cause subsequent understandings to continue and emerge; thus, it is termed "arising.
Furthermore, because it possesses the function of enabling one to realize the emergence from *nirvāṇa*, it is designated as the "cause."
The term "śramaṇa" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
this is its revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*),
for it is the Middle Way within the causes.
Regarding the reason why one is called a *śramaṇa*:
this is a detailed explanation of the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) through the term *śramaṇa*.
If there are afflictions (*kleśa*) and a lack of the path of wisdom, the afflictions are termed "deprivation" (*vaikalya*).
Furthermore, because afflictions cannot carry one far to the fruit of Buddhahood, they are called "deprivation.
One is named a śramaṇa based on that which has been abandoned [by them].
This applies from the stage of Arhat downward.
Furthermore, the light flows to the seventh person.
The four types of Arhats and others are all equally the seventh;
none of them are apart from the water of Buddha-nature.
Among them, there are those who understand and those who do not, and those who attain and those who do not;
the reason for this is not yet known.
From here on, I shall provide a detailed analysis and explanation to clarify that the two vehicles must possess Buddha-nature, and therefore it is said they are "not apart" from it.
However, because they study only partially and do not understand that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to attain such understanding,
they do not become lost or submerged in the principles and teachings of Nirvana.
The following clarifies that Arhats attain the fivefold Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the path of the four wisdoms that transcends the three realms is merely called "reaching the other shore";
it is not the ultimate ground of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is said that when the four wisdoms have illumined that which has already arisen, or the point where karma and its retribution are exhausted, this is termed "the end of my births."
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and nirvāṇa are called the "Brahman.

When the fruit of arhatship first arises through the true understanding of the path via the contemplation of emptiness, one transcends the three realms; this is called "the Brahma-faring established" (*brahmacarya-vihita*).
Subsequently, after the knowledge of exhaustion, the mind that arises takes this "established Brahma-faring" as its object; this is called "the Brahma-faring established."
When wisdom has completed the path, it is called "having done what was to be done.

When the mind arises taking as its object the path that has already accomplished what was to be done, it is called the "knowledge of having done what was to be done. This wisdom may not yet have arisen, or it may be such that one will ultimately never again undergo the fruit of future existence.
The knowledge that arises taking as its object the mind [realizing] "there will be no further existence" is called the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna). Of these,
the first and last two knowledges take the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) as their object,
while the middle two knowledges take the truth of the path (mārga-satya) as their object.
In the teachings of the past, the nirvana of the four wisdoms of the two vehicles and the three fruits of the ordinary person were termed "ultimate" and "fully endowed without remainder.
However, when discussed according to this present sutra:
Only the Buddha attains the designation of being "ultimately complete and without remainder.
The nirvana of the four wisdoms of the two vehicles is not called ultimately complete and without remainder;
however, the essence of true understanding within those four wisdoms of the two vehicles is forever absent.
Or, even if defiled, they do not lose their name of being pure.
As for these seven classes of beings who have not cultivated their bodies, precepts, minds, or wisdom, the reason they come is as illustrated by the preceding analogy of the Ganges.
In summary, these metaphors illustrate the arising of the knowledge that severs [delusion].
Those who do not understand the principle of the Middle Way and the four kinds of Buddha-nature as I have explained them become the former two types of persons;
those who can understand them become the latter five types of persons. The application of the metaphors to the persons has now been completed.
Now, [the text] summarizes these points once more to encourage their cultivation.
It clarifies that if one does not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom,
one will perpetually sink and become one of the two types of persons.
If one is able [to do so], they will surely succeed in becoming the latter five types of persons in due order.
If there should be those who say that for icchantikas and those below them, the Middle Way Buddha-nature within their clarity is neither existent nor non-existent.
Those who hold the fixed views that things definitely exist or definitely do not exist all slander the Triple Gem.
If one were to attain Bodhi without abandoning the mind of an icchantika,
this would be called defiled attachment.
If one says that [the two views] are ultimately not in conflict, it must be called false speech.
From the section on these seven types of people onwards,
the fact that they still fall back into the two aforementioned attachments which contradict reason constitutes their error.
Regarding the one who possesses seven [qualities]:
this clarifies that an icchantika who resolves their mind and cultivates wholesome deeds will proceed through a continuous succession,
eventually attaining Buddhahood after passing through the stages of the subsequent five persons.
Once [enlightenment] is accomplished, it cannot be called illusory, for each of the seven persons attains it individually.

Those who are icchantikas remain fixed in the first stage and do not belong to the latter six; they have not yet attained Buddhahood, and to claim they attain bodhi before this accomplishment would be a defiled attachment.

Because empty space currently possesses the function of allowing things to arise, whereas the Buddha-nature is not yet currently manifesting its function, it is said that it does not exist in the same way as empty space.
However, since the eternal Buddha-nature can be cultivated through the practice of goodness, it differs from a rabbit’s horn, which is ultimately non-existent. Thus, it is not like [empty space].
To say it is not non-existent is like [saying] a rabbit's horn is not non-existent.
To state that it is not called "one dharma" up to "ten thousand dharmas" clarifies that the true essence of Buddha-nature transcends all myriad phenomena.
It cannot be discussed by means of numerical quantity.
From the stage of the Vajra [Samādhi] down to the icchantika, the nature of the conditions of the five aggregates—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—is boundless.
Furthermore, it cannot be restricted by numerical quantity.
From the passage "Before attaining bodhi" onwards,
[the text] explains that this causal nature (yuanxing) is the precursor to such numerical quantity.
From the passage "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space" onwards,
this fourth major section of the chapter clarifies both the similarities and differences between Buddha-nature and empty space.
As for the reason for raising this question:

If your intention is as stated below,

In the initial inquiry, there are generally three points.

Therefore, one first challenges the meaning of the Tathāgata’s dependent origination.
For what reason is this so?
It is because if dependent origination were not sublated, self-nature would not be established; thus, one challenges it first in order to establish the intended meaning.
Second, the simultaneous arising of the body and afflictions likewise lacks causes and conditions.
Third, from "prior, posterior, or simultaneous" onwards,
it clarifies that prior, posterior, and simultaneous [arising] are all not causes and conditions, and thus they are established as being of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
As for why this person does not sever their roots of goodness,

If the nature of these five great elements were not truly produced from causes and conditions, then all phenomena would likewise exist by virtue of the same intrinsic nature as the five great elements.
As you have said, the meaning regarding the five great elements and all phenomena should be understood in this way.

If it were not so, then the aforementioned discussion on the nature of the patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*) would have been established as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based on prior causes and conditions;
now, the Tathāgata is likewise the same.
Having obtained the causal conditions,
one first destroys the nature of self-affliction.
Why is an analogy given?
Passages such as "like a drawing, like a flame," and so forth,
all clarify that all things are impermanent and in flux;
because their very substance is empty and quiescent, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding your thought that the body must come first, I have already answered the initial question below.
If you were to challenge me by saying, "If I were to claim that the body comes first," then you might find fault with my position;
however, if I were to say that the body and the afflictions each exist independently at the beginning, [then your objection would not apply].
"You may claim that the body comes first and the afflictions come later;
yet you yourself, like me, do not exist prior to your body.

My body was not there first.

the second intention clarifies the relationship between the body and the afflictions.
Although they arise simultaneously,
the mind, afflictions, and the body are established through cause and effect;
how could this possibly be their intrinsic nature?

clarifying that the principle is the cause and not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If that which is called "non-existence" is so named because the body previously lacked causes and conditions,

Regarding that which lacks causes and conditions:
you should not claim that among present phenomena, mats are made from *po* grass, cloth is produced from threads,

Since I do not perceive a self as a prior cause and condition for the mental body,
I do not say that a jar emerges from clay and so forth.
When I say that because something is perceived as an existing fact it must have a cause and condition,
you now perceive the pot;
its prior state as a lump of clay was likewise a cause and condition for it.
Why do you not apply this analogy?
Previously, you used the five great elements as an analogy for all phenomena, asserting that they are all of the nature of self;
why do you now not likewise use the jar as an analogy for the body, [showing] that it too previously arose from causes and conditions?
If you maintain that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and are devoid of causes and conditions,
for what reason do you speak of the five great elements?
On what basis do you designate that which supports as the earth element, that which moistens as the water element, that which burns as the fire element, and that which blows as the wind element?
If one says that names such as "Great Retention" (Mahādhāraṇī) refer to earth, water,

Although the five great elements as causes and conditions are thus, [the following applies].

This refers solely to form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and unmanifest action (*avijñapti*).

now, one may take the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) of all phenomena as the cause of the five great elements by analogy with those conditions being the very conditions for them.
The refutation of the five great elements as causes and conditions is now complete.

that which you identify as earth, such as the *sulāhu* resin before your eyes, [is not truly earth].

because fragrance is a quality (*guṇa*) of earth.

Second, he knew that Ānanda could not alone serve as the condition for the demons to arouse their resolve; it required the mediation of Mañjuśrī.

The reason they do not come is to demonstrate further benefit. However,

Hearing that the Buddha would enter nirvana during the latter part of the night, Ānanda did not arrive;

Before Mañjuśrī had arrived,

up until "Now, Ānanda, I am likewise endowed with these eight qualities," the Tathāgata has clearly demonstrated that Ānanda possesses the virtue of being a master of the sūtras.

Regarding this, it is said that Maudgalyāyana entered meditative absorption and saw that the Tathāgata’s mind was directed toward Ānanda.
